title: TCP U2·W4 — Tax Procedures, IRS Practice, Penalties & Ethics (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the rules of the game

Tax planning operates inside a framework of procedure and ethics — the standards a practitioner must meet, the penalties for falling short, the statute of limitations, and the examination and appeals process. A plan that ignores these is reckless: an aggressive position taken without authority exposes both the client and the preparer to penalties. This final TCP week covers Circular 230, preparer and taxpayer penalties, the limitations periods, and how disputes are resolved — the professional guardrails around everything the discipline teaches.

Circular 230 — practice before the IRS

Circular 230 (Treasury Department regulations) governs practice before the IRS by CPAs, attorneys, and enrolled agents. It imposes duties: due diligence as to accuracy, competence, prompt response to IRS requests, avoidance of conflicts of interest (waivable with informed written consent), and not charging unconscionable fees or (generally) contingent fees for preparing original returns. A practitioner who advises on a return position must have a reasonable basis and must not counsel a frivolous one. Violations can lead to censure, suspension, or disbarment from practice before the IRS — the professional license to do tax work.

Reporting-position standards

Whether a position can be taken — and whether it must be disclosed — depends on its strength, measured by escalating standards. Reasonable basis (roughly a 20% chance, the lowest defensible level) supports a disclosed position. Substantial authority (roughly 40%) supports an undisclosed position. More likely than not (greater than 50%) is required for certain positions (such as tax shelters). The planner matches the position's strength to the standard: a position with only reasonable basis must be disclosed (Form 8275) to avoid penalty, while one with substantial authority need not be. This calculus is the everyday ethics of return preparation.

Preparer penalties

A return preparer faces specific penalties. §6694 penalizes an understatement from an unreasonable position — a position lacking substantial authority (or reasonable basis if disclosed) — with a larger penalty for willful or reckless conduct. §6695 imposes per-failure penalties for procedural lapses: failing to sign the return, furnish a copy to the client, keep records, or provide a preparer identification number (PTIN), and failing to exercise due diligence on certain credits. §6713/§7216 penalize improper disclosure or use of taxpayer information. These keep the preparer accountable for both the substance and the mechanics of the return.

Taxpayer penalties

The taxpayer bears the larger penalties. The §6662 accuracy-related penalty is 20% of the underpayment for negligence, a substantial understatement (exceeding the greater of 10% of tax or $5,000), or a substantial valuation misstatement. §6663 civil fraud is 75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud. §6651 penalizes failure to file (5%/month, up to 25%) and failure to pay (0.5%/month), and an estimated-tax penalty applies to underwithholding. A reasonable cause and good-faith defense can abate many penalties — which is precisely why disclosure and documented authority matter to the planner.

The statute of limitations

The statute of limitations bounds when the IRS can assess and when a taxpayer can claim a refund. The general assessment period is three years from the later of the due date or filing. It extends to six years if gross income is understated by more than 25%, and is unlimited for a fraudulent return or a failure to file. A refund claim must be filed within the later of three years from filing or two years from payment. These periods are planning facts: they determine how long records must be kept and how long a position remains open to challenge or a refund remains recoverable.

Examination, appeals, and litigation

When the IRS examines a return (by correspondence, office, or field audit) and proposes changes, the taxpayer receives a 30-day letter offering an Appeals conference — an independent, often-favorable forum to settle on the hazards of litigation. If unresolved, a 90-day letter (statutory notice of deficiency) lets the taxpayer petition the Tax Court without first paying; alternatively, the taxpayer can pay and sue for a refund in district court or the Court of Federal Claims. Understanding this path lets a planner advise on whether to concede, appeal, or litigate, and preserves the client's rights at each deadline.

Interest, abatement, and voluntary correction

Beyond the headline penalties, interest accrues on underpayments from the due date until paid, compounding daily — so even a defensible position carries a cost if it loses. Many penalties can be abated for reasonable cause (reliance on a professional, serious illness, records lost in a disaster) shown in good faith, and the IRS offers first-time abatement for an otherwise-compliant taxpayer. When an error is found after filing, an amended return corrects it, and the IRS's voluntary disclosure programs can mitigate penalties for taxpayers who come forward before being contacted. The planner's role is to fix mistakes proactively — voluntary correction is almost always cheaper than waiting for the IRS to find the issue.

Records, representation, and privilege

Good procedure rests on records and representation. The taxpayer must substantiate income and deductions and keep records for at least the open statute period — and longer for property basis, until the asset is sold plus the limitations period. In a dispute, a CPA may represent the client before the IRS and Appeals under a power of attorney (Form 2848). A limited federally authorized tax practitioner privilege protects certain tax advice in non-criminal matters, but it does not extend to tax-return preparation or to criminal cases — so sensitive matters may warrant an attorney. Knowing the boundaries of records, representation, and privilege completes the practitioner's procedural toolkit.

CMA bridge

For a CFO signing MBG's returns and dealing with the IRS, Circular 230, the position standards, and the penalty regime are the professional boundaries of tax planning — they define how aggressive a position can be and what must be disclosed. The CFO who plans within these rules, documents authority, and knows the audit-and-appeals path protects both the company and the preparer, the professionalism TCP instills.

Practice and recap

  1. Follow Circular 230 (due diligence, competence, conflicts, fee limits); violations risk censure/suspension/disbarment.
  2. Match positions to standards: reasonable basis (≈20%) → disclose; substantial authority (≈40%) → undisclosed OK; more likely than not (>50%) for shelters.
  3. Know preparer penalties (§6694 unreasonable position, §6695 procedural) and taxpayer penalties (§6662 20% accuracy, §6663 75% fraud, §6651 file/pay).
  4. Apply the statute of limitations (3 yr general; 6 yr if >25% omission; unlimited for fraud/non-filing; refund: later of 3 yr from filing / 2 yr from payment); navigate exam → 30-day letter → Appeals → 90-day letter → Tax Court.

Recap: tax practice is bounded by Circular 230's duties and by reporting standards (reasonable basis requires disclosure, substantial authority does not, more-likely-than-not for shelters); preparers face §6694/§6695 penalties and taxpayers face the §6662 20% accuracy, §6663 75% fraud, and §6651 failure-to-file/pay penalties (abatable for reasonable cause); the statute of limitations runs three years generally, six if income is understated by more than 25%, and unlimited for fraud or non-filing, with refund claims due within three years of filing or two of payment; and disputes flow from examination through a 30-day letter and Appeals to the 90-day notice of deficiency and the Tax Court — the procedural and ethical framework around all tax planning.
